The de-skilling of work and workers’ loss of control

rationales.A: The passage says wages were low, not steadily rising for all.
rationales.B: The passage describes factory work growing, not ending.
rationales.C: A craftsman who set his own pace has lost skill and control: machines broke his craft into one repeated task, which is de-skilling.
rationales.D: The passage is about factory work, not a return to farming.
rationales.general:
Name the change behind the example.
1. The craftsman once set his own pace, which took skill and judgment.
2. Now he repeats one task at a machine for hours.
3. The skill is gone from his day, and so is his control of the pace.
4. That loss of skill and control is what historians call de-skilling.
Remember: one worker’s day can illustrate a change across a whole economy.

source: original; stimulus verified against its source (see source_note)
stem: The passage describes a craftsman who once set his own pace now repeating one task at a machine. Which broader change in Gilded Age work does that best illustrate?

stimulus.source_note: Original secondary passage, written for this question from Barron’s Premium 2027 Chapter 8 (Topic 6.7), 5 Steps to a 5, 2024, Chapter 18, and Princeton Review, Chapter 10.
stimulus.text:
Original secondary passage, written for this question from the grounding books:

As factory work was broken into simple, repeated tasks, employers hired more women and children, whose pay was lower than men’s. Families often needed the extra wages because a working-class man’s pay alone was low. By 1900, children aged ten to fifteen made up 18 percent of the industrial workforce, and women made up 17 percent. Machines also took skill out of work: a craftsman who once set his own pace now repeated one task at a machine for hours, and unsafe mills and mines injured workers in large numbers.
